corpus_definition: A person who helps someone else in their work.

forms.definition: a person whose job is to help another person with their work
forms.example: The doctor's assistant called me to change the time of my visit.

syn.note: Easy, general word; a helper is not always paid, an assistant usually has a job.
Used mostly for people who help politicians or important officials.
A deputy is second in charge and can take the boss's place; an assistant just helps.
A secretary does office work like letters and phone calls; an assistant can help with many kinds of work.

ant.note: The boss gives the orders; the assistant helps the boss.

forms.definition: help or support that you give to someone
forms.example: If you need any assistance, please ask at the front desk.

syn.note: Everyday word with the same meaning; assistance is more formal.
Support can also mean help with money or feelings.
Often used for help given to countries or people in trouble.

ant.note: Something that makes a job harder instead of easier.

forms.definition: to help someone do their work or a job
forms.example: Two nurses assisted the surgeon during the operation.

syn.note: Everyday word; assist is more formal.
Support can also mean helping with money or feelings.
Formal, often used in news and official writing.

ant.note: To make it harder for someone to do something.

forms.note: Assistant is used before other nouns (assistant manager, assistant teacher), but learner dictionaries list it as a noun, not a separate adjective.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My aunt works as an assistant at a bank in Tashkent. She assists the manager with letters and meetings. When customers need assistance, they often come to her first.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays the noun-slot main entry; assistance is an extra noun. Assistant before a noun (assistant manager) is treated as noun use, not an adjective.

corpus_definition: A person who is very good at sports.

forms.definition: a person who is good at sports and often takes part in competitions
forms.example: Many young athletes from Uzbekistan train hard for the Olympic Games.
forms.note: In British English it often means a runner, jumper or thrower; in American English it can be any sports player.

syn.note: A man who plays sports; for a woman, sportswoman. Athlete is used for both.
Easy word: a person who plays a game or team sport, like football.
One kind of athlete: a person who runs in races.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: physically strong, fit and good at sports
forms.example: My brother is very athletic; he plays football and swims every day.
forms.note: Also means 'connected with sports': an athletic club.

syn.note: Easy and a little informal: someone who likes and is good at sports.
Fit means healthy and strong from exercise, not always good at sports.
Easy word: having a powerful body.

ant.note: Not healthy or strong because you don't exercise.

forms.definition: in a way that shows a strong, fit body and sports skill
forms.example: She is athletically gifted and won three races this year.

syn.note: In a way connected with the body, not only sports.

people.definition: sports such as running, jumping and throwing
people.example: Our school has a big athletics competition every spring.
people.note: American English often says track and field.

context.text: Dilnoza is a young athlete from Fergana. She is very athletic and trains every morning before school. Next month she will run in the national athletics championship.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, kept as noun main entry; athletics goes to People & things as the field.

corpus_definition: Sports such as running, jumping, and throwing.

forms.definition: sports such as running, jumping and throwing, often in competitions
forms.example: She competes in athletics for her school in Samarkand.
forms.note: Uncountable and used with a singular verb: athletics is popular. British English; American English usually says track and field.

syn.note: The American name for the same sports.
Easy, general word for all games and physical activities.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: connected with running, jumping and other sports, or good at them
forms.example: The city opened a new athletic stadium last year.

syn.note: Connected with sport: a sporting event.
Easy and informal: describes a person who likes sports.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with sports or a fit body
forms.example: He is not very tall, but he is athletically strong.

syn.note: In a way connected with the body, not only sports.

people.definition: a person who is good at sports and takes part in races
people.example: Every athlete in the team must train six days a week.

context.text: Athletics is my favourite school sport. Our athletic coach says every athlete must warm up before a race.

reviewer_note: British/American trap: athletics (UK) = track and field (US); in American English athletics can mean all sports.

corpus_definition: A place or thing that people like to visit for fun.

forms.definition: an interesting place or thing that many people go to see
forms.example: The Registan is the most famous tourist attraction in Samarkand.
forms.note: Also means a feeling of liking someone romantically; that is a different meaning.

syn.note: Usually plural: the sights of a city are its famous places.
A famous building or place that is easy to see and recognize.
A phrase used in guidebooks; a little formal.

forms.definition: to make people want to come to a place or see something
forms.example: The old city of Khiva attracts thousands of visitors every year.

syn.note: Draw people or crowds means the same; a little informal.
Easy phrasal verb: the festival brings in many tourists.
Informal: to get a lot of people to come.

ant.note: To make people or things go away or stay away.

forms.definition: pleasant or interesting, so that people want it or like it
forms.example: Low hotel prices make Bukhara attractive to young travellers.
forms.note: Also means good-looking when it describes a person.

syn.note: Pleasant and interesting; very close in meaning.
Easy word: makes you want to know or see more.
So attractive that you want to have or do it, even if you shouldn't.

ant.note: Not pleasant or interesting, so people don't want it.

forms.definition: in a pleasant way that makes people interested
forms.example: The rooms were attractively decorated with Uzbek carpets.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word.
Stronger: very pleasant to look at.

context.text: The new water park is the biggest attraction in our town. It attracts families from all over the region, and the cheap tickets make it even more attractive.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: attraction = a place to visit, not romantic attraction; forms are anchored to drawing visitors.

corpus_definition: uncomfortable or embarrassing; not smooth or easy

forms.definition: the feeling of being uncomfortable or embarrassed in a situation
forms.example: There was some awkwardness when we met my ex-boss at the wedding.

syn.note: The feeling when you are shy or ashamed in front of others.
Not feeling relaxed; can also mean a small pain.
Moving in a way that is not smooth, so you drop or hit things.

ant.note: Feeling relaxed and comfortable with people.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.

forms.definition: making you feel uncomfortable or embarrassed; also not smooth or easy
forms.example: There was an awkward silence after his strange comment.

syn.note: Easy word: not feeling relaxed.
Making you feel shy or ashamed; a little stronger.
About movement: not smooth, so you drop or hit things.
Easy word: not easy to do or deal with.

ant.note: Relaxed and at ease with people.
Moving in a smooth, beautiful way.

forms.definition: in an uncomfortable or embarrassed way, or in a way that is not smooth
forms.example: He smiled awkwardly when the teacher read his poem to the class.

syn.note: In a way that shows you don't feel relaxed.
About movement: not smoothly, often dropping or hitting things.

ant.note: In a smooth and beautiful way.

context.text: At the party I didn't know anyone, so I felt a bit awkward. I stood awkwardly in the corner until my friend Aziz arrived.

reviewer_note: The corpus definition joins two ideas (embarrassing and not smooth); synonyms and antonyms cover both. -ward is not in the affix table, so no affix is claimed on the base.

corpus_definition: The bags and suitcases you carry when traveling.

forms.definition: all the bags and suitcases that you take on a trip
forms.example: Please collect your baggage in the arrival hall at Tashkent airport.
forms.note: Uncountable: say 'a piece of baggage', not 'a baggage'.

syn.note: Same meaning; luggage is more common in British English, baggage at airports and in American English.
Easy everyday word: 'Where are your bags?'
One large case with a handle; baggage means all your bags together.

forms.note: There is no verb in this family.
There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: We had too much baggage for the train to Bukhara. Each passenger can take only two pieces of baggage, so my mother left one box at home.

reviewer_note: Countability trap: baggage is uncountable. -age is not in the affix table, and the link to bag is not a clear derivation, so no affix is claimed.

corpus_definition: A state where things are equal and not falling over.

forms.definition: the ability to stay steady and not fall over
forms.example: She lost her balance on the ice and fell down.
forms.note: Common phrases: keep your balance, lose your balance. It also means the money in a bank account; that is a different meaning.

syn.note: Being steady and not likely to move or fall; a little formal.
Being firm and not shaking.
Scientific or very formal word for the same idea.

ant.note: A state where things are not equal or not steady.
Not being steady; likely to fall or change.

forms.definition: to stay steady or keep something steady without falling
forms.example: The waiter balanced three plates on one arm.

syn.note: To stop something from shaking or falling.
More formal; British spelling: stabilise.
Easy word: to keep something in your hands or in one place.

ant.note: To fall over, or make something fall over.

forms.definition: with all parts equal or in the right amounts
forms.example: A balanced diet has fruit, vegetables, bread and some meat.

syn.note: Easy word: equal on both sides.
Firm and not moving or shaking.
About opinions or news: showing all sides equally.

ant.note: With some parts too big or too small, or not steady.

forms.note: There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My little sister is learning to ride a bike, but she keeps losing her balance. Dad says she must balance with her body and keep her weight balanced on both sides.

reviewer_note: Three corpus rows have the same meaning and share one map (all B1). Bank-account balance is a different meaning and is not used. -ed is not in the affix table, so balanced gets no affix.

corpus_definition: A person who cuts hair for men.

forms.definition: a person whose job is to cut men's hair and shave beards
forms.example: I go to the barber near the bazaar once a month for a haircut.
forms.note: 'At the barber's' means at the barber's shop (British English).

syn.note: Cuts hair for women and men; a barber usually works only with men.
A modern word for someone who cuts and styles hair.

forms.note: There is no common verb in this family; people say 'cut hair'.
There is no adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: My grandfather has visited the same barber for twenty years. The barber knows exactly how he likes his beard.

reviewer_note: False-suffix trap: barber is not barb + -er, so no affix is claimed. Headword is a person noun and stays the noun main entry; barbershop is a compound and is left out.

corpus_definition: a line of light, or a long strong piece of wood or metal

forms.definition: a line of light, or a long heavy piece of wood or metal in a building
forms.example: A beam of sunlight came through the window.
forms.note: In buildings, beams hold up the roof or floor.

syn.note: A thin line of light: a ray of sunshine.
A shaft of light is a long, narrow line of it; a little literary.
Easy, general word.
For the wood or metal meaning: a long, straight piece of something hard.

forms.definition: to send out light or radio signals
forms.example: The sun beamed down on the cotton fields all afternoon.
forms.note: Beam also means 'to smile widely and happily'.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word for giving out light.
For signals: to send out on radio or TV.

forms.definition: smiling widely because you are very happy
forms.example: The beaming parents took photos of their son at graduation.
forms.note: Belongs to beam = smile widely, not a line of light or a piece of wood.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: Our old house in Margilan has wooden beams across the ceiling. In the morning the sun beams through the small window, and a bright beam of light falls on the floor.

reviewer_note: The corpus definition joins two meanings (light, and wood or metal); one row, so one map labelled Light that mentions both. Beaming (smiling) is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: the front part of the human body below the chest

forms.definition: the front part of your body between your chest and your legs
forms.example: The boy has a pain in his belly after eating too much plov.

syn.note: The most common, neutral word.
Informal, often used by or with children.
Medical or very formal word.

ant.note: The back is the part of the body on the other side, behind you.

forms.note: There is no common verb in this family.
There is no common adjective in this family.
There is no adverb in this family.

context.text: After the big wedding dinner, my uncle said his belly was full. He lay on the sofa and patted his round belly.

reviewer_note: Register trap: belly is informal; stomach is the neutral word. Belly button is a compound and is left out.
